shi01.summary: A five-character old-style poem in the voice of a wife thinking of her husband, who has gone far away. It begins with a parting as final as death, uses the northern horse and the southern bird to say that every creature longs for home, then turns to her own wasting away, and ends by comforting herself: 'eat well'. The words are plain and the feeling runs deep. It opens the Nineteen Old Poems.
shi01.translation:
On and on, and on and on you go,
parted from me, a living separation.
Ten thousand li and more lie between us,
each of us at a different edge of the sky.
The road is steep and long,
how can we know when we will meet again?
The horse of the north leans into the north wind,
the bird of Yue nests on the southern branch.
Every day we are further apart,
every day my belt hangs looser.
Floating clouds hide the white sun,
the traveller does not think of turning back.
Thinking of you makes me grow old,
the months and years are suddenly late.
Let it be, I will not speak of it again,
I will try my best to eat my meals.

glossary.note: Parting while both people are still alive, which can feel as hard as a parting by death. The Chuci (Songs of Chu) has the line: 'No sorrow is greater than a living parting'.

glossary.en: hu ma yi bei feng - 'the northern horse leans into the north wind'
glossary.note: A horse from the north, even when taken south, still leans towards the north wind. It stands for people who never forget their homeland.

glossary.en: Yue niao chao nan zhi - 'the bird of Yue nests on the southern branch'
glossary.note: Yue is the far south. A southern bird still builds its nest on the branch facing south. Like the horse, it stands for longing for home.

glossary.en: fu yun bi bai ri - 'floating clouds hide the white sun'
glossary.note: Clouds hiding the sun was a common image for slanderers blocking a worthy person from the ruler. Here most readers take it to mean that the traveller has been led astray by distractions and does not come home.

glossary.en: bu gu fan - 'does not think of returning'
glossary.note: The traveller does not think of coming back. The character for 'return' here is an old form of the usual one.
To throw aside, to leave behind: she tells herself to stop dwelling on it and not speak of it again.

shi01.background: The Nineteen Old Poems are anonymous. They are usually thought to be by scholars of the middle and later Eastern Han dynasty (25-220), and were later collected in the Wen Xuan, an anthology compiled by Xiao Tong (501-531). Later poets treated them as the model of the five-character poem.

shi02.summary: A five-character old-style poem about a woman who was once a singing girl and is now the wife of a man who roams far from home. She stands alone in an upstairs window in spring. Six lines of doubled words paint her beauty, and the last two say plainly that an empty bed is hard to bear. Loneliness and resentment show through the contrast.
shi02.translation:
Green, green, the grass along the riverbank,
lush, lush, the willows in the garden.
Graceful is the woman in the upper room,
bright and pale she stands at the window.
Lovely, lovely, in her rouge and powder,
slender, slender, she stretches out a white hand.
Once she was a singing girl,
now she is the wife of a wanderer.
The wanderer goes and does not come home,
the empty bed is hard to keep alone.

glossary.note: Describes a lovely bearing and a graceful way of carrying oneself.
Describes something white and shining; here it is her face in the window light.
Describes a lovely face and appearance.
Describes fingers that are long, fine and soft.
A woman from a family of singers and dancers. The word 'chang' is an old variant of another character and in early times meant an entertainer who sang and danced.
A man who leaves home and roams without returning. This is the old meaning of the word, not the modern 'dissolute person'.

shi03.summary: A five-character old-style poem. It starts from cypress and stone, which seem to last for ever, and sets against them a human life as brief as a traveller's stop. From that it argues for enjoying oneself while one can, and describes the splendour of Luoyang, with its princes' mansions and towering palace gates. The last line, 'what presses on you so?', shows that the pleasure still carries a note of unease.
shi03.translation:
Green, green, the cypress on the mound,
heaped up, the stones in the mountain stream.
Human life between Heaven and earth
is suddenly like a traveller going far.
A dou of wine for each other's pleasure,
let us take it as generous rather than meagre.
Driving a cart behind a poor horse,
we wander for fun to Wan and to Luo.
How lush and bustling is Luoyang,
officials in cap and sash seek each other out.
Long avenues run beside lanes,
princes and lords have many great houses.
The two palaces gaze at each other from afar,
the twin gate towers are a hundred feet and more.
Feast to the full and please the heart,
why be so anxious, what presses on you?

glossary.en: hu ru yuan xing ke - 'suddenly like a far traveller'
glossary.note: A picture of how short life is: we pass through the world quickly, like a guest on the road.
A dou is a measure for wine; here it means only a small amount, a modest drink.
Wan is Nanyang and Luo is Luoyang, both famous cities of the Eastern Han dynasty (25-220). Luoyang was the capital.
The dress of officials, so it means high officials and the well-born.
The Southern Palace and the Northern Palace of Luoyang.
Describes a restless, worried state of mind.

shi04.summary: A five-character old-style poem about a happy banquet. It first praises the zither music and the way host and guests understand each other, then sighs that life is short and urges people not to stay poor and low, but to take a place of power while they can. It shows how scholars of the late Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD) felt, pulled between the wish for fame and the brevity of life.
shi04.translation:
At today's fine banquet
the joy is hard to tell in full.
The zither is played, its sound rises free,
the new tune is so fine it enters the spirit.
A man of virtue sings lofty words,
those who know music hear the truth in them.
All of one mind, with the same wish,
yet what is in the heart is not fully said.
A human life is lodged in one age,
suddenly gone like dust in a whirlwind.
Why not whip up the swift horse
and first seize the main road and the ford?
Do not stay poor and lowly,
long in hardship and bitter toil.

glossary.en: ling de - 'a person of fine virtue'
glossary.note: Fine moral character; here it means a person who has it.

glossary.en: shi qu ting qi zhen - 'one who knows the tune hears its truth'
glossary.note: Only a listener who understands music can hear what the tune really means.
In an instant, swiftly.
Dust thrown up by a violent wind, a picture of a life that is short and uncertain.

glossary.en: yao lu jin - 'the main road and the ford'
glossary.note: The important roads and river crossings, standing for a position of power and influence.
The same as the common word for 'rough going'. It stands for a person whose hopes are not met.

shi05.summary: A five-character old-style poem about sad music heard from a high tower. The poet sighs that a true listener, one who understands, is so rare, and in the end imagines turning into a pair of calling cranes that fly up together with a kindred spirit. Through the music it speaks of talent unrecognised and of loneliness, and the mood is lofty.
shi05.translation:
In the north-west there is a high tower,
its top level with the floating clouds.
Crossed lattices carved like patterned silk on the windows,
the hall has eaves on all four sides, and three flights of steps.
Above, the sound of strings and singing,
how sad the notes are.
Who could play such a tune?
Could it be the wife of Qi Liang?
The clear shang melody drifts out on the wind,
the middle of the song lingers and turns.
One pluck, and she sighs three times,
stirring and fierce, with grief left over.
I do not pity the singer her pain,
I only grieve that those who understand are so few.
I wish we could be a pair of calling cranes,
beat our wings and rise to fly high.

glossary.en: jiao shu jie qi chuang - 'lattice windows patterned like silk'
glossary.note: The windows are carved into crossing lattices that look like the pattern of fine silk.

glossary.en: e ge - 'a hall with eaves on four sides'
glossary.note: A tower or pavilion with roofs sloping on all four sides.

glossary.en: Qi Liang qi - 'the wife of Qi Liang'
glossary.note: In the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC), Qi Liang of the state of Qi died in battle. His wife wept so hard for him that, according to legend, the city wall fell down.
A kind of ancient music with a clear, sad tone.

glossary.en: zhi yin - 'one who knows the tune'
glossary.note: Someone who understands music; later, a close friend who truly understands you.

glossary.en: shuang ming he - 'a pair of calling cranes'
glossary.note: Two cranes calling to each other, a picture of kindred friends who share the same ideals.

shi06.summary: A five-character old-style poem about crossing the river to pick lotus flowers to give to someone far away, with no way to deliver them. Looking back towards home, the road is endless. The two are of one heart but live apart, and can only grow old in sorrow. The tone is sad and restrained.
shi06.translation:
I cross the river to pick lotus flowers,
in the orchid marsh there are many fragrant plants.
Who do I pick them to give to?
The one I miss is on a distant road.
I turn and look back towards my old home,
the long road stretches vast and without end.
One in heart, yet living apart,
I will grow old in sorrow.

glossary.en: she jiang - 'to wade across the river'
glossary.note: To cross the river.
The lotus. Here the word means the flower of the lotus, not the hibiscus it can mean today.
A marsh or water meadow where orchids grow.
To present something as a gift.

glossary.en: tong xin er li ju - 'one in heart but living apart'
glossary.note: Their hearts are the same, but they cannot live together.

shi07.summary: A five-character old-style poem that begins with an autumn night scene and sighs at how the seasons change. It then complains that a former schoolmate, now successful, has forgotten old ties, and uses the names of stars, the Winnowing Basket, the Dipper and the Ox-Driver, to say that a name can be empty. The scene sets the mood for the poet's disappointment at how coldly the world treats the poor.
shi07.translation:
The bright moon shines white, the night is full of light,
the crickets chirp by the east wall.
The Jade Beam of the Dipper points to early winter,
how clearly the many stars stand out.
White dew wets the wild grass,
the season has suddenly changed again.
Autumn cicadas cry among the trees,
the swallows have left, and where have they gone?
Once my friend from the same teacher's door
rose high and beat his six strong feathers.
He does not think of how we once walked hand in hand,
he throws me away like a footprint left behind.
In the south there is the Winnowing Basket, in the north the Dipper,
and the Ox-Driver star does not pull a yoke.
It is true there is no friendship firm as a great rock,
so what good is an empty name?

glossary.note: A cricket. The name means 'urging the weaving', because its song was heard as a call to hurry with the autumn cloth.
The fifth star of the Big Dipper. Scholars have long disagreed about which month the poem means by the direction it points.
The swallow, which flies south for the winter.

glossary.en: liu he - 'the six large wing feathers'
glossary.note: The six large feathers of a bird's wing, standing for a strong pair of wings.

glossary.en: nan Ji bei you Dou - 'the Winnowing Basket in the south, the Dipper in the north'
glossary.note: The stars called the Winnowing Basket and the Dipper do not live up to their names: the basket cannot winnow and the dipper cannot scoop. They stand for something with a name but no substance.

glossary.en: Qian Niu bu fu e - 'the Ox-Driver does not carry the yoke'
glossary.note: The star named after an ox-driver pulls no cart. It is another image of a name without the reality behind it.

shi08.summary: A five-character old-style poem about a newly married woman who is far from her husband and anxious, but still hopeful. She likens herself to a lone bamboo and the dodder clinging to its host, and fears that her youth will pass and the flower bloom with no one to pick it. At the end she says that if he holds firmly to his principles, she can only wait patiently.
shi08.translation:
Slender and drooping, a bamboo growing alone,
it has set its roots in a bend of Mount Tai.
I am newly married to you,
like the dodder clinging to the pine moss.
The dodder has its season to grow,
husband and wife should meet at the proper time.
We married across a thousand li,
far apart, with mountain slopes between.
Thinking of you makes me grow old,
why is your carriage so late in coming?
I grieve for those orchid blossoms,
holding their petals, spreading their light.
If the season passes and they are not picked,
they will wither with the autumn grass.
You truly hold to your high principles,
and what can a humble wife like me do?

glossary.note: Describes something slender, weak and hanging down.
A curve or fold in a mountain, where a plant can take root.
A parasitic plant, often a thread-like vine, that twines around other plants. Here it stands for a bride who depends on her husband.
Another plant that grows on others, such as on pine trees.
A hillside; the second character can also mean a pond.
A carriage with a screen or curtains. Here it is the carriage that would come to fetch the bride.

shi09.summary: A five-character old-style poem in which a woman breaks off a blossom from a rare tree in her courtyard, meaning to send it to someone far away, but the road is too long for her to do so. The close says the flower is nothing special, only that she grieves at how long they have been apart. A small flower carries a great deal of longing.
shi09.translation:
In the courtyard there is a rare tree,
its green leaves are full of rich blossom.
I pull down a branch and break off the flowers
to give to the one I think of.
The fragrance fills my bosom and sleeves,
but the road is far and I cannot send it.
What is there to prize in such a thing?
It only moves me that we have been parted for so long.

glossary.note: A tree that is unusual and seldom seen.
Flowers in full, lush bloom. The first character is the old way of writing the word for 'flower'.
Flowers. An old distinction: herbs 'hua', trees 'rong'.

glossary.en: yi suo si - 'to give to the one I think of'
glossary.note: To send a gift to the person she misses.

glossary.en: jing shi - 'a long time has passed'
glossary.note: Much time has gone by.

shi10.summary: A five-character old-style poem that uses the legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl to speak of the pain of longing. The two stars face each other across a clear, shallow Milky Way, looking with love but unable to speak. The doubled words are used with great skill, and the poem gently speaks for husbands and wives parted in the human world as well.
shi10.translation:
Far away is the Ox-Driver star,
bright is the Weaver Girl of the River of Stars.
She lifts her slender, pale hands,
the loom clacks and clacks as she works the shuttle.
All day long she weaves no pattern,
tears fall like rain.
The River of Stars is clear and shallow,
how far apart are they, then?
Just one brimming stretch of water lies between,
they look at each other with feeling and cannot speak.

glossary.note: Describes a great distance.

glossary.en: He Han nu - 'the girl of the River of Stars'
glossary.note: The Weaver Girl, a star in the constellation Lyra. 'He Han' is the Milky Way.
To draw out or reach out a hand.
The sound of the loom at work.
The weaving loom and the shuttle that carries the thread.
Looking at someone silently, full of love.

shi10.background: One of the Nineteen Old Poems. It uses the legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, who are allowed to meet only once a year, to express the longing of married couples who are parted.

shi11.summary: A five-character old-style poem. On a long journey by carriage the poet looks around at a wide, empty view, and nothing he meets is as it once was. He feels how quickly life passes and that rise and decline each have their time, and he ends by encouraging himself to treasure a good name. Behind it lies a deep sadness about the shortness of life.
shi11.translation:
I turn my carriage round and set out,
far and long I travel the road.
I look all around, how vast and empty it is,
the east wind stirs the many grasses.
Everything I meet is not what it was,
how can I not grow old fast?
Rise and decline each have their time,
my only fear is making my name too late.
Human life is not metal or stone,
how could it be long?
Suddenly we change away with all things,
so an honoured name is the real treasure.

glossary.en: hui che - 'to turn the cart around'
glossary.note: To turn the carriage head round and set off on a new road.

glossary.en: jia yan mai - 'to drive on far'
glossary.note: To drive off on a long journey. The middle character is just a filler word, and the last means 'to go far'.
Things as they used to be.
To live to a great age.

glossary.en: wu hua - 'to change away with things'
glossary.note: A way of saying someone dies: they pass away as all things change.
A good reputation, a name that is remembered with respect.

shi12.summary: A five-character old-style poem. The changing seasons make the poet sigh at the passing of time and urge himself not to shut his feelings up. The second half turns to a beauty of Yan and Zhao playing a tense string tune, which stirs him so that he wishes he were a pair of swallows carrying mud to build a nest, a picture of longing for a happy bond.
shi12.translation:
The eastern city wall is high and long,
winding along, joined end to end.
A whirlwind stirs and rises from the ground,
the autumn grass is thick and still green.
The four seasons change in turn,
how swiftly the year is drawing to its end.
The morning-wind bird holds a bitter heart,
the cricket grieves at its cramped life.
Better to wash it all away and let the feelings go,
why bind yourself up?
In Yan and Zhao there are many beauties,
the loveliest have faces like jade.
Dressed in robes of fine silk,
they sit at the door and play a clear tune.
How sad the sound is,
the strings are tight, so I know the bridges are pressed close.
My heart is racing, I straighten my belt,
humming low, I pace to and fro.
I wish I were a pair of flying swallows,
carrying mud in my beak to nest in your house.

glossary.note: Describes something that curves and runs on in one long line.
The name of a bird, often thought to be a kind of hawk.
Narrow, confined, with no room to stretch.
To wash clean; here it means to rinse away one's sorrow.
Two states of the Warring States period (475-221 BC) in the north-east of China. Ancient writers said many beautiful women came from there.
The movable bridge that holds up the strings of a zither. When the bridges are close together the strings are tight.

shi13.summary: A five-character old-style poem. The poet drives to the east gate of Luoyang and looks far off at the graves of Beimang to the north. He sighs that life is short, that even sages cannot escape death, that seeking immortality with elixirs mostly goes wrong, and that one may as well drink good wine. The tone is bleak and passive, and shows how scholars at the end of the Han thought about life and death.
shi13.translation:
I drive my carriage up to the East Gate
and look far off at the graves north of the city.
How the white poplars rustle,
pines and cypresses line the broad road.
Below lie the long dead,
dim and dark in an endless night.
They sleep deep beneath the Yellow Springs,
for a thousand years they will not wake.
Vast, the yin and yang pass on and change,
life is brief as the morning dew.
Human life is suddenly like a lodging,
and no age is firm as metal or stone.
Generation after generation sees the last one off,
sages and wise men cannot cross over.
Some take elixirs to seek the immortals,
and most are ruined by the drugs.
It is better to drink fine wine
and dress in silk, plain or patterned.

glossary.en: Shang Dong Men - 'the Upper East Gate'
glossary.note: One of the three gates on the east side of the Luoyang city wall, the northernmost.

glossary.en: guo bei mu - 'the graves north of the city'
glossary.note: The burial grounds on the north side of the city, the Beimang hills.
The underworld, where people go after death.

glossary.en: nian ming ru zhao lu - 'life is like morning dew'
glossary.note: Life is as brief as dew that dries in the morning sun.
To swallow alchemical drugs in search of long life.

glossary.en: wan yu su - 'fine silks, plain and patterned'
glossary.note: Fine silk fabrics, standing for rich and beautiful clothing.

shi13.background: The Beimang hills north of Luoyang have been a burial ground since ancient times.

shi14.summary: A five-character old-style poem. Outside the city the poet sees nothing but mounds and graves, old tombs ploughed into fields and pines and cypresses cut for firewood, with a sad wind in the poplars. This leads him to reflect on how people vanish, and to the sorrow of having no way home. The landscape is bleak.
shi14.translation:
Those who have gone grow more distant day by day,
those who live grow dearer day by day.
I go out of the outer gate and look straight ahead,
and see only mounds and graves.
The old tombs are ploughed into fields,
the pines and cypresses are broken up for firewood.
In the white poplars there is much sad wind,
it rustles and rustles and grieves a man to death.
I long to go back to the lanes of my village,
but there is no way for me to return.

glossary.note: People who have passed away, the dead.

glossary.en: guo men - 'the gate of the outer wall'
glossary.note: A gate in the outer wall of a city.
Wood used as fuel.
To make someone terribly sad. The second character here only strengthens the first, as an intensifier.
A village or neighbourhood; here the poet's old home.

shi15.summary: A five-character old-style poem whose point is that life is short, so there is no need to carry worries meant for a thousand years. The day is short and the night is long, so why not light a candle and wander? It argues against miserliness, and adds that the immortal Prince Qiao cannot be waited for. The tone is blunt and carefree.
shi15.translation:
Our years of life do not reach a hundred,
yet we often carry the worries of a thousand years.
The day is short and we suffer from the long night,
why not take a candle and go out to enjoy ourselves?
To be happy one should seize the time,
how can we wait until next year?
The foolish man holds dear his money and goods,
and is only laughed at by later ages.
The immortal Prince Qiao
is hard to arrange to wait for.

glossary.en: bing zhu you - 'to wander holding a candle'
glossary.note: To go out at night carrying a candle, a way of saying that one does not want to waste any time.
The coming year.
To laugh at someone, to ridicule.
A legendary immortal. He is said to have been Prince Jin, the crown prince of King Ling of the Zhou dynasty (c. 1046-256 BC), who became an immortal and left the world.
To agree to wait for someone. The poet means that one cannot wait to become immortal like Prince Qiao.

shi16.summary: A five-character old-style poem. In the cold at the end of the year a woman sleeps alone through the long nights and dreams that her husband comes in his carriage to take her home. On waking she finds no one there, and can only weep at the door. It tells of longing through a dream, with feeling that turns and turns again.
shi16.translation:
Bitter cold, the year is said to be ending,
the mole cricket cries sadly at dusk.
The cool wind has already turned fierce,
the traveller is cold and has no clothes.
The brocade quilt was left by the banks of the Luo,
the one who shared my robe has gone against my wish.
I lie alone night after night,
in dreams I long to see your shining face.
My husband remembers our old joy,
he stoops to drive here and hands me the rope for the carriage.
I wish to see your clever smile always,
to go home with you in one carriage, hand in hand.
You came, but stayed only a moment,
and you did not stay in the inner room.
It is true I have no wings like the morning-wind bird,
how could I fly up against the wind?
I glance around to console myself,
and stretch out my neck to gaze far off.
I pace to and fro, my heart sorrowful,
tears fall and wet both doors.

glossary.note: An insect that calls in the evening.
Largely, almost all. Here it says that the cool wind has become fierce everywhere.

glossary.en: jin qin yi Luo pu - 'the brocade quilt left by the Luo bank'
glossary.note: Left by the bank of the Luo River. Commentators explain this in different ways: roughly, either the husband has gone far and not returned, or an old keepsake has been left somewhere else.

glossary.en: tong pao - 'one who shares a robe'
glossary.note: Originally soldiers who shared one battle cloak. Here it means the husband.
The rope handed to someone to pull themselves up into a carriage.
The deep women's quarters of a house, a bedroom.

shi17.summary: A five-character old-style poem about a cold winter night of sorrow. She watches the moon wax and wane, and a letter comes from far away. She keeps it so close that its words stay clear after three years. She ends by saying that her heart is wholly true and she fears only that the other will not understand.
shi17.translation:
At the start of winter the cold has come,
how bitter the north wind is.
Grief is heavy and I know how long the night is,
I look up at the stars in their rows.
On the fifteenth the bright moon is full,
on the twentieth the toad and hare are missing.
A traveller came from far away
and left me a letter.
The top lines speak of long longing,
the lines below of long parting.
I put the letter in my breast and sleeve,
after three years the writing has not faded.
With one heart I hold this small devotion,
and fear that you will not see and understand it.

glossary.en: meng dong - 'the first month of winter'
glossary.note: The tenth month of the lunar calendar, the beginning of winter.
Cold and biting.
Fifteen: the fifteenth day of the lunar month, when the moon is full.
Twenty: the twentieth day of the lunar month, when the moon has begun to wane.
A poetic name for the moon. In Chinese legend a toad and a jade hare live in the moon.
A small but heartfelt offering of feeling.

shi18.summary: A five-character old-style poem in which a traveller from far away brings a length of patterned silk. The woman makes it into a quilt with a pair of mandarin ducks, fills it with long silk floss and edges it with a knot that cannot be undone, and finishes by comparing her bond to glue dropped in lacquer, which nothing can part.
shi18.translation:
A traveller came from far away
and left me a length of patterned silk.
Ten thousand li and more lie between us,
still my old friend's heart is just so.
The pattern is a pair of mandarin ducks,
I cut it into a quilt of joy and union.
I fill it with long, long floss for longing,
and edge it with a knot that cannot be untied.
With glue thrown into lacquer,
who could part them?

glossary.en: yi duan qi - 'a length of figured silk'
glossary.note: A piece of patterned silk. 'Duan' is a measure for lengths of cloth.

glossary.en: he huan bei - 'a quilt of joy and union'
glossary.note: A quilt embroidered with matching patterns, a symbol of a husband and wife in harmony.
To stuff the quilt with silk floss.
The word for silk thread sounds like the word for longing, so the long silk threads stand for long-lasting longing.
To sew along the border of the quilt.

glossary.en: yi jiao tou qi zhong - 'glue thrown into lacquer'
glossary.note: Once glue and lacquer are mixed they cannot be separated. It stands for a bond that is firm and cannot be broken.

shi19.summary: A five-character old-style poem about a sleepless night under the moon. The poet gets up and paces, and thinks that however pleasant life away may be, it is better to go home soon. In the end he goes out the door, has no one to tell, and returns to his room with tears on his clothes. The words are plain and the feeling deep. It is the last of the Nineteen Old Poems.
shi19.translation:
How bright and white the moon is,
it shines on my bed's silk curtains.
Sorrow keeps me from sleeping,
I put on my clothes, get up and pace.
The life of a traveller is said to be happy,
but it is better to turn back home early.
I go out the door and wander alone,
to whom can I tell my grief?
I stretch my neck to look, then go back inside,
tears fall and wet my robes.

glossary.en: luo chuang wei - 'the silk bed curtains'
glossary.note: The gauze curtains of a bed.

glossary.en: lan yi - 'to put on one's clothes'
glossary.note: To throw on or straighten one's clothing.
Being on a journey, living away from home.
To go home without delay.

glossary.en: pang huang - 'to pace, unable to decide'
glossary.note: To walk back and forth, not knowing where to go.
To crane one's neck and look far off.
